core: Precise legal/operational definitions of refugee, asylum-seeker, internally displaced person (IDP), and how they differ from a (voluntary/economic) migrant
The 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol
Major causes of forced displacement: conflict, persecution, disaster, and increasingly climate
The scale of global forced displacement, attributed to UNHCR with its date

Composition of the global total: IDPs as the majority; refugees; asylum-seekers

claims.claim: The 1951 Refugee Convention defines a refugee as a person outside their country of nationality owing to a well-founded fear of being persecuted for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, or political opinion, who is unable or unwilling to return.
The 1951 Convention was originally limited to events in Europe before 1951; the 1967 Protocol removed the temporal and geographic limits, making the definition universal.

Article 33 of the 1951 Convention establishes non-refoulement: no state shall expel or return a refugee to the frontiers of territories where their life or freedom would be threatened on account of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, or political opinion.
An asylum-seeker is a person whose claim to protection has not yet been decided; because refugee status is declaratory, asylum-seekers should be treated as refugees until determined otherwise.
An internally displaced person is forced to flee but has not crossed an international border and remains within their own country.

'Migrant' is an umbrella term with no internationally accepted legal definition, covering people who move within a country or across a border for many reasons; it carries no automatic entitlement to international protection.
At the end of 2024, UNHCR estimated about 123.2 million people were forcibly displaced worldwide, roughly one in every 67 people.

Internally displaced people were the largest displaced group at the end of 2024, about 73.5 million (close to 60 percent of the total); refugees and others in need of international protection numbered about 42.7 million.
The largest forced-displacement situations at the end of 2024 were Sudan, Syria, Afghanistan, and Ukraine; most refugees are hosted by low- and middle-income countries.

People displaced by disasters or climate change generally do not fit the 1951 Convention definition because they are not persecuted on one of the five grounds; many become IDPs or, if they cross a border, are classified as migrants.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the ~123 million total should be quoted as the mid-2024 (122.6 million) or end-2024 (123.2 million) figure.
positions: UNHCR Mid-Year Trends 2024 reported 122.6 million forcibly displaced as of mid-2024
UNHCR Global Trends covering 2024 (released June 2025) reported 123.2 million at the end of 2024
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the most recent authoritative figure, 123.2 million at the end of 2024 from Global Trends (released June 2025), and rounds to 'about 123 million' with an explicit date and attribution.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The '1 in X people' ratio is reported against different reference points in coverage.
positions: UNHCR's 2024 reporting states roughly 1 in 67 people worldwide were forcibly displaced
A decade earlier the ratio was about 1 in 114
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson quotes 'roughly one in every 67 people' tied to UNHCR's 2024 reporting, without over-precise framing.

correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated boilerplate entirely with sourced legal definitions and dated figures.
Ensured every displacement statistic carries a date and UNHCR attribution.
Added the precise refugee/asylum-seeker/IDP/migrant distinctions and the disaster/climate legal gap that the boilerplate omitted.
rightsIssues: Primary sources (UNHCR pages/reports, IOM glossary, the 1951 Convention text) are treated as REFERENCE_ONLY. Facts and definitions were synthesized into original prose; no source wording was reproduced beyond short standard legal phrasing of the Convention definition, which is the treaty text itself.

UNHCR web hosts (unhcr.org) blocked the automated fetcher (HTTP 403); the figures and definitions were verified via web search corroboration across multiple independent reports of the same UNHCR data and via the reachable emergency.unhcr.org guidance page. Canonical UNHCR URLs are recorded; the notes state which copy was actually read.

sourceRecords.title: Convention and Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees (1951 Convention and 1967 Protocol)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the Article 1A(2) refugee definition (well-founded fear of persecution on five grounds, outside country of nationality), the 1967 Protocol's removal of temporal/geographic limits, and Article 33 non-refoulement. The unhcr.org host returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher; the Convention text (Art. 1A(2) and Art. 33(1)) was verified through web-search corroboration quoting the treaty and cross-checked against the reachable emergency.unhcr.org refugee-definition page. Canonical UNHCR PDF: https://www.unhcr.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/1951-refugee-convention-1967-protocol.pdf

sourceRecords.title: Refugee definition (UNHCR Emergency Handbook)
sourceRecords.notes: Fetched successfully. Supports the operational distinctions among refugee, asylum-seeker, and IDP; the declaratory nature of refugee status (asylum-seekers treated as refugees until determined otherwise); the 1967 Protocol's universalizing role; and the regional broadenings (1969 OAU Convention, 1984 Cartagena Declaration).

sourceRecords.title: Global Trends: Forced Displacement in 2024
sourceRecords.notes: Released 12 June 2025. Supports: ~123.2 million forcibly displaced at end of 2024; roughly 1 in 67 people; IDPs ~73.5 million (~60% of total); refugees and others in need of international protection ~42.7 million; largest situations Sudan, Syria, Afghanistan, Ukraine; most refugees hosted by low- and middle-income countries. unhcr.org blocked the fetcher (HTTP 403); figures verified via web-search corroboration across multiple independent reports (UNHCR press release, USA for UNHCR, Al Jazeera) citing the same UNHCR data. Canonical report PDF: https://www.unhcr.org/sites/default/files/2025-06/global-trends-report-2024.pdf

sourceRecords.title: Key Migration Terms
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the definition of 'migrant' as an umbrella term not defined under international law, covering people moving within a country or across borders for varied reasons, and the point that migrant status carries no automatic international protection (distinguishing migrants from refugees). Verified via web-search corroboration quoting the IOM glossary.
